newsitem.title: FRANCE: Criminal investigation started on Credit Lyonnais.
newsitem.headline: Criminal investigation started on Credit Lyonnais.

text.p: The Paris public prosecutor opened a criminal investigation on Monday into suspected fraud and the issuing of misleading information at state bank Credit Lyonnais in the early 1990s, justice sources said.

The move followed a request by Finance Minister Jean Arthuis in August for legal proceedings against former top managers at the bank, which was brought to its knees with massive losses in the early 1990s.

The sources said the investigation had been opened against persons unknown, a procedure under which an investigating magistrate seeks to determine possible criminal responsibility before a possible prosecution of named individuals.

Arthuis said in August he wanted to bring former bosses -- he mentioned no names -- to justice for failing to keep control of subsidiaries during a runaway expansion in the late 1980s and early 1990s which briefly made Credit Lyonnais the biggest bank outside Japan.
Credit Lyonnais was headed between 1988 and 1993 by Jean-Yves Haberer, who was appointed by the former Socialist government and has since been replaced by Jean Peyrelevade.
Arthuis said at the time that some 15 inquiries were under way abroad and 27 in France but these focused on subsidiaries such as Altus Finance rather than the parent company.
He wanted the issue taken higher to establish jurisprudence on legal accountability of company bosses at the top level.
Justice Minister Jacques Toubon asked the public prosecutor's office in mid-August to look into the request.

Credit Lyonnais revealed losses of 21 billion francs ($4 billion) between 1992 and 1994 and has since been steered from one salvage plan to another, with a third rescue expected soon that could take government aid well to over 100 billion francs ($20 billion), according to some estimates. ($1=5.225 French Franc)
